paras: The lynching of Felix Barnes, also reported as Gus Barnes, was the killing of a young Black man by a party of citizens near Sparta, Georgia, in late March 1881. Accused of attacking a young white woman named as Miss Lizzie Johnson, he was pursued, caught, hanged and shot. Dispatches from Sparta, Atlanta and Macon carried the story across the country, and the Atlanta version reported that the killing was approved locally and that 'nothing will be done'.

According to a Macon dispatch, Barnes, a man of about twenty, was said to have attacked Miss Johnson on a Thursday as she walked on a road near the town's suburbs, knocking her down and beating her before two men answered her cries and he ran away. A fuller version of that dispatch said she fought him off until passing men rescued her. The Atlanta wire, by contrast, said that he 'outraged the person of' Miss Johnson, while the Sparta dispatch spoke of an 'outrage attempted' by a youth of eighteen about five and a half miles from town. The Macon account called Barnes 'a bad character' and added that his father had once represented the county in the Legislature.

A party was organized at once to pursue him. The Sparta dispatch, the earliest report in print, said that on Wednesday night about 9 o'clock more than twenty 'of the best people in the neighborhood' caught him, tied a rope around his neck, carried him into the woods and hanged him. In the Atlanta version the citizens hanged him to a tree and then filled his body with bullets.

The Macon dispatch told it differently: the pursuers came back without Barnes, and the next day his body, riddled with bullets and with the head nearly severed, was brought into Sparta on a wagon from the spot where the attack was said to have happened. That dispatch said only that he was 'supposed' to have been captured, brought back and executed there, and that his friends and family followed the body with 'noisy cries of grief'. A Delaware brief alone said that he had been 'arrested', identified and had confessed, saying 'the devil entered him', before he was found hanging the next morning.

The Atlanta dispatch said the lynching was 'sustained by public sentiment' and that 'nothing will be done', and the Sparta dispatch said the 'swift punishment' was 'not condemned'. No report of an inquest, an arrest or a prosecution appears in the coverage, and none of the killers was named.

Only the white press covered the killing, starting with the Sparta dispatch to the Augusta Evening News that the Savannah Morning News reprinted on March 26. The Atlanta wire ran in the New York Sun under 'The Lynching of a Negro', in the Chicago Daily Tribune under 'LYNCHED', and in the Washington Evening Star, all treating the accusation as 'the crime'. Where the Sun had 'sustained by public sentiment', the Tribune printed 'regarded as justifiable'.

The Macon version appeared in the Delaware Daily Gazette under 'MURDER AND OUTRAGE IN GEORGIA' and in Alexandria as 'SWIFT RETRIBUTION', and was reprinted in New Jersey and Maryland. Another Delaware paper, the Daily Republican, headed its brief 'Summary Punishment'. Into mid-April, small papers in Tennessee, Arkansas, Rhode Island, South Carolina and elsewhere ran one- or two-sentence briefs, one describing 'a beautiful young white girl', without comment.

The reports differ on the victim's first name, Felix in the Atlanta dispatch and Gus in the Macon one, and on his age, eighteen or about twenty. They also differ on the date: the Sparta dispatch put the hanging on Wednesday night (March 23), a Maine brief on Thursday night, the Macon dispatch put the alleged attack on Thursday with the body found the next day, and the Atlanta wire put the attack on Friday (March 25). The Sparta and Macon accounts, the closest to the scene, describe an attempted assault and are the more specific, but no account says who saw the killing.

reader.title: Lynching of Felix (Gus) Barnes
bases: Every account has a party of private citizens catching an accused Black man near Sparta, Georgia, and killing him by hanging and/or shooting without any legal process (A1, A2, A5).

A Sparta dispatch says a party of 'over twenty' men hanged the accused youth in the woods (A1), and the Atlanta and Macon dispatches describe a citizens' party that pursued, caught and killed him for an alleged assault on a white woman, with no officers or legal proceedings mentioned (A2, A5).

Separate Sparta/Augusta (A1), Atlanta (A2) and Macon (A5) dispatches agree that an accused Black man was caught and killed by a party of citizens near Sparta, though they differ on his first name, the dates and the manner of death.

accounts.label: Sparta dispatch to the Augusta Evening News
accounts.gist: A young Black man of eighteen was accused of attempting an 'outrage' on a white girl about five and a half miles from Sparta; on Wednesday night about 9 o'clock more than twenty men caught him, put a rope around his neck, carried him into the woods and hanged him.

accounts.label: Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: Felix Barnes was accused of assaulting Miss Lizzie Johnson of Sparta; indignant citizens pursued and caught him, hanged him to a tree and filled his body with bullets, and nothing would be done.

accounts.label: Macon dispatch
accounts.gist: Gus Barnes, about twenty, was accused of knocking down and beating Miss Johnson on a road near the suburbs on Thursday; a party pursued him and came back without him, and the next day his body, shot and with the head nearly severed, was brought into Sparta on a wagon from the spot of the alleged attack; he was 'supposed' to have been captured and executed there.

accounts.label: Delaware brief ('Summary Punishment')
accounts.gist: The accused fled, 'was arrested', was identified and was said to have confessed, saying 'the devil entered him'; the next morning he was found hanging from a tree, shot.

framing.detail: The Atlanta dispatch called the citizens 'indignant', treated the accusation as 'the crime', and said the lynching was 'sustained by public sentiment' (Sun) or 'regarded as justifiable' (Chicago Tribune).
The Sparta dispatch described a 'diabolical outrage', called the lynchers 'the best people in the neighborhood' and the victim 'the criminal', and said the 'swift punishment' was 'not condemned'.
The Macon dispatch ran under 'MURDER AND OUTRAGE IN GEORGIA' in a Delaware paper, called Barnes 'a bad character', said his execution was only 'supposed', and noted his family's grief.
Small-town papers in Tennessee, Arkansas, Rhode Island, South Carolina and elsewhere ran one- or two-sentence briefs, without comment, in general news columns into mid-April.
